posts.body:
We're running with more buyer and lease leads than we can work right now. Mostly new construction in San Antonio and Austin, plus out-of-state relocations. They're warm but they need vetting and nurture. Most aren't ready to move today.

If this sounds like something you'd take on, send me a DM.

I joined my team because I was tired of grinding alone. First month here, a deal went sideways. Inspection issues, appraisal came in low, seller got defensive. Instead of watching it die, three agents stopped what they were doing and sat down with me. We worked through it together. Deal closed. That's when it hit me. This isn't about the split or the marketing budget or whatever your last broker promised. It's about being surrounded by people who actually show up for you. Who care if you win or lose. Who believe your success is their success. Most agents never experience that. They move from broker to broker chasing commission splits and never ask the real question. Who has my back when things get hard. At Lifestyle Design Realty, that's the baseline. Not the perk.

We're running with more buyer and lease leads than we can work right now.

Mostly new construction in San Antonio and Austin, plus out-of-state relocations. They're warm but they need vetting and nurture. Most aren't ready to move today. That's the honest part. These aren't hot leads sitting on your desk waiting to convert tomorrow. They're real people in real situations who need someone to stay in front of them, build trust, and be ready when they're actually ready to move. If you're the kind of agent who can work a long pipeline and turn patient follow-up into closed deals, this is exactly the kind of volume you should have in your business.

If this sounds like something you'd take on, send me a DM.

I used to think my split was the problem. Moved three times chasing a better percentage. Never got better. Then I realized the real issue. I was working alone without support, accountability, or people who cared if I won. The split didn't matter because I had nothing backing me up.

Had a listing this week where the agent almost walked because the seller was indecisive. First offer came in 15k below asking. Instead of letting it die, we pulled in our negotiation person and had a strategy call the same day. Seller got clarity. Second offer came in 8k higher. Deal closed. 1. Most agents handle objections alone and lose deals they could have saved. Having someone to sense-check with changes everything. 2. Speed matters. We moved on a solution the same day instead of waiting for the agent to figure it out solo. 3. The agent stayed confident because she knew she wasn't the only one problem-solving. That confidence shows up in how you communicate with clients. This is what separates agents who move deals from agents who lose them?

We have more buyer and lease leads than we can actually work right now.

New construction in San Antonio and Austin mostly, plus out-of-state relocations coming in. They're warm leads but they need vetting and real nurture work. Most of them aren't ready to close today. That's the honest part. These are people in transition who need someone to stay consistent with them until they're actually ready to move. If you're an agent who knows how to work a pipeline and turn patience into closed deals, this is the volume you should have in your business.

If this sounds like something you'd take on, send me a DM.

I hit a wall last month. Commission was solid but I was burnt out. Same routines. Same problems. No one pushing me to think bigger. I realized I wasn't growing anymore. I was just maintaining.

That's when I knew it was time to move.

If you're telling yourself you're fine where you are but you're not excited about tomorrow, that's a sign. If your broker hasn't invested in your growth in the last year, that's a sign. If you're making decent money but feel invisible, that's a sign.

Outgrowing a place doesn't mean the place is bad. It means you're ready for more.

The question isn't whether you should leave. It's whether you're brave enough to admit you've already left mentally?
